stories.title: What the Fire Kept
passages: Nora Callahan stood in the doorway of the Maple Street bakery at five in the morning and could not make herself step inside. The smell reached her first — scorched sugar and wet plaster — before her eyes adjusted to the dark shapes of the ovens, blistered and black, and the collapsed shelf where her mother's recipe box had sat for eleven years. A firefighter's boot prints tracked ash across the floor in drying puddles. She had signed the lease renewal three days ago. She had spent the evening proofing dough for the Bellhaven Hotel tasting, the one that would have paid off the last of her mother's debts, and left it rising under a damp cloth she now found melted into the counter. The electrician had warned her about the wiring back in March. She had put it off, the way she had put off crying at the funeral, the way she had put off answering the calls from the bank. Now the recipe box, her mother's handwriting looping across index cards stained with vanilla and butter, was a block of soaked ash she could not bring herself to touch. Nora sat down on the curb outside, still in yesterday's apron, and did not call anyone for a long time.

Three days after the fire, Nora Callahan sat across a metal desk from an insurance adjuster who kept using the word "depreciated" as if it were a kindness. The payout, when it came, would cover perhaps a third of what she needed to replace the ovens, and not until the claim cleared underwriting, a process he estimated at ten to twelve weeks. Her landlord had already re-listed the unit, citing a damage clause she hadn't read closely enough. At the bank, a loan officer she had known since high school slid her file back across the counter and said the words "not without collateral" with visible discomfort. Nora spent the afternoon in her car in the parking lot, making a list of things she could sell: the mixer she had bought secondhand, her grandmother's ring, the bakery's domain name, which a competitor had already emailed twice to buy. She called her cousin Denise to ask about the couch in her spare room, and tried to keep her voice even when Denise asked how bad it really was. That night she ate crackers standing at the counter of the rented room, too tired to feel the humiliation fully, just carrying it, the way she had once carried flour sacks, one at a time.

By the second week of April, Nora Callahan had settled into a rhythm at Fenn's Wholesale Bakery, where she worked the four-to-midnight shift portioning dinner rolls onto trays for grocery store delivery. The work was steady and required nothing of her creativity: measure, cut, place, repeat, four hundred times a shift. Her coworkers were friendly enough, trading stories about weekend plans and a manager's tendency to overorder cinnamon. Nora ate her break sandwich in the stairwell most nights, scrolling through apartment listings without much urgency, since the room above Denise's garage suited her fine for now. She had stopped checking the insurance portal every hour, mostly because there was nothing new to see there. Twice she drove past the boarded storefront on Maple Street out of habit rather than longing. On Thursdays she did laundry at the place on Ash Avenue and read paperbacks while the machines ran. She sent her aunt a birthday card two days late. The city had scheduled a farmers market for the summer, and a flyer for vendor applications sat on her kitchen table for a week before she used the back of it to write a grocery list, not yet deciding whether she wanted a stall there at all.

On a whim, or something close to one, Nora Callahan filled out the vendor application after all and paid the modest deposit for a stall at the Saturday farmers market. She spent her one day off baking in Denise's kitchen, three dozen brown-butter cookies and a tray of hand pies, and drove them to the market before dawn with the trays balanced on the passenger seat. By ten o'clock she had sold out. A man named Feliks, who ran a well-regarded bistro two blocks from the old bakery, stopped at her table twice, bought a hand pie both times, and on the second visit asked whether she would consider baking for him on a standing order, starting small: two dozen rolls a day, paid weekly, no contract required yet. Nora said yes before she had entirely thought it through. She spent that evening doing math on the back of a receipt, and for the first time since the fire the numbers, though small, moved in the right direction. She texted Denise a photograph of the empty trays with three exclamation points. Word got around the market faster than she expected, and by the following Saturday she had a line before the stall was even set up.

Feliks called on a Tuesday to say that a friend of his, a producer for a regional food program called The Kitchen Line, had eaten one of Nora Callahan's hand pies at the bistro and wanted to feature her in an episode about bakers rebuilding after loss. Nora had to sit down on Denise's kitchen floor while he explained it a second time. Two days later, the same afternoon the insurance settlement finally cleared, a small-business grant she had applied for in a fog of exhaustion back in April came through as well, enough, combined with the payout, to lease a smaller storefront on Birch Street and buy a secondhand oven in good condition. She stood in the empty space that evening with Denise and Feliks, the three of them eating pizza off the box balanced on a windowsill, and Nora found she was laughing at nothing in particular, the ordinary giddy laughter of disbelief. She called her aunt and, for the first time in months, cried from something other than grief. That night she taped a photograph of her mother above where the new register would go, and slept better than she had in a year.

The morning the crew from The Kitchen Line filmed at the new shop on Birch Street, Nora Callahan wore her mother's apron, mended at the pocket, and welcomed a line that stretched past the corner before she had even unlocked the door. Feliks came by with a bucket of peonies for the counter and stayed longer than the delivery required, long enough that Denise raised her eyebrows across the room. The producer asked Nora to talk about the recipe box, and instead of the ash and ruin, she found herself telling the crew about her mother's handwriting, and how a neighbor who had salvaged three warped cards from the wreckage had returned them to her, laminated, the week before. She read the cinnamon roll recipe into the camera and her voice did not shake. By afternoon she had sold every pastry twice over, rationing what remained, and strangers were photographing the window display of her mother's photograph beside the register. That night the whole street seemed to know her name. Feliks stayed to help her stack chairs after closing, and when he finally left, Nora stood alone in the swept, flour-dusted kitchen, full to the brim with something she had not let herself feel in a long time: pure, uncomplicated pride.

Six weeks into running the Birch Street shop, Nora Callahan had traded one kind of exhaustion for another. The television segment had brought a steady run of new customers, which meant longer hours, which meant she had hired her first employee, a nineteen-year-old named Trevor who was diligent but still learning to laminate dough without tearing it. She spent most mornings on payroll spreadsheets she did not fully understand and afternoons retraining herself to bake in a kitchen laid out differently from the one she had lost. Feliks still came by most days, though their conversations had settled into something comfortable rather than charged, more about wholesale pricing than anything else, and Nora was not sure yet what to make of that. The flour supplier switched brands without telling her, and her bread came out slightly different for a week before she diagnosed why. None of it was catastrophic. She renewed her business insurance, this time reading every clause twice, and filed the paperwork for a second oven on layaway. Some nights she was too tired to tell whether the shop was thriving or merely surviving, and simply closed up, drove home, and slept.

A local food blog ran a review of the Birch Street shop under the headline "Charming Story, Uneven Execution," and Nora Callahan read all eleven hundred words of it standing at the register before opening. The critic praised the story and the peonies and then spent four paragraphs describing a batch of croissants — the batch Trevor had made alone while she trained a new hire — as dense and underproofed. By noon, three separate customers had mentioned the review to her, one apologetically. Feliks called to say it did not matter, that one review never sank a good bakery, but his voice had an edge of concern he was not quite hiding. That afternoon the flour supplier called to say her account, still new, would be put on hold pending a credit check, a formality, he said, though it meant she could not place Thursday's order. Nora spent the evening testing croissant batches until nearly midnight, flour ghosting her sleeves, trying to find exactly where the process had gone wrong, and could not. She thought, standing over the fourth failed batch, of the recipe cards, and wondered, not for the first time that week, whether she had rebuilt the shop faster than she had rebuilt herself.

The credit hold on Nora Callahan's flour account stretched into its second week, and the workaround, buying retail from a restaurant supply store an hour away, was eating into margins she could not afford to lose. Trevor gave his notice, apologetically, for a job with steadier hours near his college, and she had not yet found anyone to replace him. The grant money was gone, spent on the oven and the first month's deposits, and the loan she had taken to cover the gap between the settlement and the true cost of rebuilding came due for its first payment on the fifteenth, a date that now sat on her calendar like a stone. Feliks's wholesale order, still her most reliable income, was paid net-thirty, which meant the money existed only on paper for weeks at a time. Nora sat with the ledger at midnight, the shop dark around her, and could not make the numbers agree no matter how she arranged them. She thought about the bakery on Maple Street, gone now to a vape shop, and wondered whether she had simply built a smaller version of the same collapse. For the first time since the fire, she let herself imagine closing the doors for good.

Denise sat with Nora Callahan at the kitchen table on a Sunday and went through the ledger line by line, the way she did spreadsheets for her own job, and by the end of it the numbers looked less like a stone and more like a hill, steep but not vertical. They worked out a stricter schedule for the wholesale invoices, and Denise offered to handle the bookkeeping in exchange for a standing supply of the brown-butter cookies. Nora placed a smaller, cash-only order with the retail supplier to bridge the two weeks until the credit hold cleared, and posted a hiring notice at the community college where Trevor had enrolled. A woman named Priya, recently laid off from a downtown café, answered by the end of the week and started training on a Tuesday. The loan payment went through, tight but on time. Feliks, without being asked, adjusted his order terms to net-fifteen once she mentioned the cash flow problem, calling it a fix to an oversight on his end rather than a favor. None of it solved everything, but the ledger closed that month in Nora's favor by a small, real margin, and she allowed herself to notice it.

By early autumn, Nora Callahan had settled Priya into the morning shift and found, to her surprise, that the woman had a gift for laminated dough that made Trevor's early efforts look tentative by comparison. The flour supplier lifted the credit hold after a clean three months of payment history, and her margins evened out enough that she could finally set aside a small cushion each week instead of watching the account hover at zero. Feliks asked her to cater a private anniversary dinner for one of his regulars, her first catering job, and it went well enough that the guests asked for her card. The food blog that had run the harsh review published a follow-up piece, unprompted, noting the improvement in her croissants and crediting the new hire's technique alongside her own; Nora read it twice and felt something in her chest unclench that she had not realized was still tight. She began, tentatively, sketching plans for a second oven line and a small seating area by the window, nothing official yet, just measurements in a notebook. On the anniversary of the fire, she baked a small cake for no one but herself and Denise, and it felt less like mourning than she had expected.

A year to the week after the fire, Nora Callahan reopened the expanded shop on Birch Street with a seating area, a hand-lettered sign that read Callahan's, and her mother's three salvaged recipe cards framed above the register beside the newer photograph from the television segment. The morning crowd spilled onto the sidewalk, and Denise handled the register while Priya and a second new hire ran the kitchen, giving Nora room to stand at the door and greet people by name, something she had never had time for before. Feliks arrived with peonies again, and this time he stayed the whole afternoon, and when he took her hand behind the counter during a lull, unhurried and certain, Nora felt no need to overthink it the way she once might have. The loan was more than halfway paid. A regional bakers' association had asked her to speak at their spring conference about rebuilding a business from nothing. Late that evening, after the last customer left and the chairs were stacked, Nora stood in the quiet kitchen with Denise and Feliks, the ovens warm, the recipe cards catching the last light, and felt, without needing to measure it, that she had finally built something that would hold.

stories.title: The Ninety-Day Wind
passages: Eleanor Bramwell stood in the mud at the edge of the airstrip and watched the last of the wreckage being dragged off the field, the biplane's wing spars snapped like kindling where the hailstorm had caught it three nights before, tied down in the open because the hangar roof had failed the winter before and there had never been money to fix it. Her father had died on the Tuesday between the storm and the wreckage removal, his heart giving out in the kitchen while totaling what the repairs would cost, and the county coroner's certificate sat unsigned on the table because Eleanor could not make herself carry it into town. The bank's letter had arrived that morning, forwarded from the house because she had not been home: the note on Bramwell Field was called due in full, ninety days, over the missed spring payment. She had exactly one flyable plane left, an old trainer with a cracked cowling, and forty-one dollars in the cigar box her father had used for the till. The mechanics who had worked the field for a decade did not come in that morning, unsure whether there was anything left to come in for. Eleanor sat down on the running board of the truck and did not move for a long time.

Eleanor Bramwell drove to Prairie State Bank on Thursday in her father's good coat and asked to speak with the loan officer, a man named Hollis who had known her father for twenty years and still would not meet her eyes across the desk. The bank could not extend the note, he said, not with the collateral damaged and no cosigner, and he suggested, not unkindly, that she consider what the land alone might fetch. She spent the afternoon at the county recorder's office confirming what she already feared, that the field and the house sat on the same parcel, tied together by her father's one stroke of bad paperwork years before. At the hardware store, the owner let her charge a tarp and two gallons of dope for the wing fabric but would not extend further credit, citing his own creditors. She drove home past the Hargrove place, where an auction notice was staked in the yard, and did not stop to look at it long. That night she sat at her father's desk going through the hangar's remaining inventory, an engine block, some fabric, tools, tallying what she could sell without also selling the last chance of keeping the field, and found the total came to very little.

By the middle of June, Eleanor Bramwell had arranged enough odd work to keep the lights on without touching the ninety-day clock ticking down on the mortgage. Three mornings a week she flew the trainer over Kessler's wheat fields, dusting for chinch bugs at a rate per acre that barely covered the fuel, and in the afternoons she did engine work for a rancher two counties over who paid in cash and mutton. She had grown used to the rhythm of it: up before light, the cold cockpit, the long straight passes over the fields, home by mid-morning smelling of chemical dust. Hollis at the bank had stopped calling, which she took as neither good news nor bad. She wrote her aunt in Wichita a letter that said less than it could have and mailed it without rereading it. The hangar sat mostly empty now, swept clean, the wreckage finally hauled to the scrapyard for what little it brought. In the evenings she read the aviation trade papers her father had subscribed to, out of habit more than hope, and one Tuesday noticed, without much reaction at first, a notice for a cross-country air derby out of Wichita with a purse of two thousand dollars for the winner.

Eleanor Bramwell read the derby notice three more times before she let herself consider it seriously: a cross-country race from Wichita to Cheyenne and back, open to licensed pilots, entry fee twenty-five dollars, first prize two thousand. It was, she calculated at the kitchen table twice, almost exactly what remained on the mortgage after the interest. She spent two weeks stripping the trainer down herself, replacing the cracked cowling with one welded by the rancher she had been doing engine work for, a quiet man named Walt Pruitt who refused payment and instead asked to come along as her mechanic if she qualified. The plane, lighter and better tuned than it had flown in years, took the qualifying trial at the county field on a clear Saturday morning, and Eleanor came in under the required time by nearly four minutes, fast enough that the officiating steward asked her to repeat the run to be sure his stopwatch had not erred. Walt whooped from the sideline in a way she had not heard from anyone in months. That evening she wired the entry fee to Wichita before she could talk herself out of it, and drove home with the truck windows down, the summer air loud around her, feeling, for the first time since the storm, something like forward motion.

The morning of the derby's opening leg, a man in a good suit introduced himself to Eleanor Bramwell as a representative of Halloway Oil and asked whether she had a sponsor for the aircraft's fuel and lettering. She had not, and braced for the conversation to end there, but he offered the company's backing on the spot, seventy-five dollars and free fuel along the whole route, in exchange for the company's name painted along the fuselage, a piece of luck so unlikely that Walt made her repeat the terms twice to be sure he had not misheard. She wired the news to her aunt in Wichita, who wrote back by return post with two exclamation points and a five-dollar bill folded in for luck. The lettering went on the plane that afternoon, and standing back to look at it, bright against fabric her own hands had stretched and doped, Eleanor felt something loosen in her chest that had been tight since the night of the storm. Walt cooked supper over the field's fire pit that evening, and pilots from other entries came by to trade stories, and for the first time in a year, Eleanor laughed until it hurt, sitting in the dark with people who did not know enough about her troubles to be careful around her.

Eleanor Bramwell crossed the checkpoint at Cheyenne eleven minutes ahead of the nearest competitor, and the small crowd at the airfield cheered loudly enough that she heard them over the engine before she had even cut it. A newspaperman took her photograph beside the Halloway Oil lettering, and Walt, grinning wider than she had ever seen him, ran out to check the undercarriage before she had finished climbing down. That night the derby organizers held a dinner in the town hall for the leading pilots, and Eleanor sat with fliers whose names she recognized from her father's trade papers, several of whom asked, without condescension, about her turn radius and fuel mixture. A young pilot named Robert Iversen, flying for a rival oil company, teased her about her lead over supper and later walked her out to look at the stars, admitting he hoped she would hold it, since beating her would then mean something. Walt wired news of the standing back to the Bramwell Field hands, and word reached Hollis at the bank, who, Walt reported with satisfaction, had asked after her with what sounded almost like pride. Eleanor slept that night better than she had in a year, half from exhaustion and half from something like happiness.

The morning after Cheyenne, Eleanor Bramwell spent three hours with Walt going over the engine before the return leg, a routine check that turned up a hairline crack in one of the cylinder fins, not dangerous yet but worth watching over the remaining miles. Robert Iversen's crew loaned them a spare part from their own stores, a gesture Walt accepted with more reservation than gratitude, muttering afterward that rival teams did not usually hand out favors for nothing. The derby route for the return leg had been changed overnight because of weather reports over the western stretch, adding forty miles and a fuel stop that had not been part of the original planning, which meant recalculating the fuel mixture Eleanor had only just settled on. She wired Walt's cousin in Denver to confirm the new fuel stop actually existed and was stocked, a detail the derby office had been vague about. None of it was alarming exactly, just the ordinary friction of a race with more legs still to fly than already flown. She ate breakfast without much appetite, thinking about the cylinder fin more than the standings, and by the time she took off for the next leg, the lead she had built at Cheyenne felt less like a cushion and more like a number that could still change.

The cylinder fin gave out over open range forty miles short of the rescheduled fuel stop, and Eleanor Bramwell brought the plane down dead-stick onto a stretch of pasture, jarring but level, her hands steadier than she felt. It took six hours for Walt to reach her by truck with the spare part and another four to make the repair properly in the fading light, time that dropped her from first to fourth in the standings by the derby office's telegraphed update. Worse news waited at the next checkpoint: a telegram from Hollis at the bank, forwarded twice to catch up with her, stating that the ninety-day grace period would not be extended regardless of the derby's outcome, some confusion at the bank's head office having overridden the local branch's earlier leniency. Robert Iversen's team had moved into the lead outright, and the Halloway Oil representative, reached by telephone, was polite but noncommittal about what continued sponsorship might depend on. Walt did not say much on the drive to the hotel that night, which Eleanor had learned by now meant he was more worried than he wanted to show. She lay awake doing arithmetic that would not resolve, the derby's remaining purse against the mortgage deadline, and could not make the two numbers meet no matter how she arranged them.

By the penultimate checkpoint, Eleanor Bramwell had fallen to sixth place, and the fuel money from Halloway Oil had been quietly reduced, a company man explaining by wire that the sponsorship terms were tied to standing in the top three. The mortgage deadline now sat eleven days out, well before the derby's final purse would be paid even if she somehow won it outright, a timing problem she and Walt had not thought to check when they first entered. Walt suggested wiring Hollis to ask, one more time, for even a week's grace, and the bank's reply came back within the day: regretfully, no exceptions, head office's instruction. Robert Iversen found her outside the hangar that evening and, gently enough, said he had heard about the mortgage from someone at the fuel depot, and that he was sorry, in a tone that made clear he understood there was nothing to be done about it from where he stood. Eleanor sat with Walt on the tailgate of the truck long after dark, the cracked-fin repair holding but the plane otherwise tired, and admitted, quietly, that the arithmetic no longer worked no matter how she arranged it. She pulled on her jacket the next morning anyway, before dawn, because sitting still had started to feel worse than flying.

Walt drove into town the next morning without telling Eleanor Bramwell where he was going, and returned at noon with news that he had found her aunt's cousin, a grain elevator operator named Simmons who held some standing with the regional bank that had recently absorbed two of Prairie State's smaller notes, Eleanor's among them in the reshuffling. Simmons could not promise anything, but he agreed to wire the regional office directly to ask whether the derby's final payout, expected within three weeks of the deadline, could be accepted as settlement if she finished anywhere in the paid places, rather than requiring the full sum on the original date. The regional office's answer, when it came, was noncommittal but not a refusal: they would consider a short extension given proof of expected income. It was not the guarantee Eleanor wanted, but it was more room to breathe than she had had in days. Robert Iversen's mechanic, without much comment, returned the spare cylinder fin part they had borrowed earlier along with a second one as backup, waving off Walt's attempt to pay for it. Eleanor spent that evening rechecking the plane herself, methodically, the cracked fin repair holding steady, and allowed herself to think, cautiously, that the last two legs of the race might still matter.

On the second-to-last leg, Eleanor Bramwell flew the tightest course she had all derby, cutting closer to the checkpoints than she had dared before, and climbed back to third place by the time she landed, close enough behind Robert Iversen and the leader that the derby office noted it as a real contest again in the evening standings. Simmons wired to say the regional bank had accepted the arrangement formally, in writing, conditional on her finishing in the paid positions, which meant the mortgage no longer depended on winning outright, only on holding her place. Walt found no new trouble in the engine that night, the cylinder fin repair having held clean through the hardest flying of the week, and allowed himself, for the first time since the crack, to talk about the last leg in terms of strategy rather than survival. Halloway Oil's representative wired to say the company would resume full sponsorship terms if she held top three through the finish, a reversal Eleanor read twice to be sure of. She wrote her aunt a longer letter than usual that night, and slept with the window open, the prairie air cool and full of the smell of the next morning's weather, feeling something she recognized, cautiously, as hope rather than mere relief.

Eleanor Bramwell crossed the final line in Wichita in third place, close enough behind the leaders that the crowd cheered for her nearly as loud as for the winner, and Walt was running alongside the taxiing plane before the propeller had fully stopped. The purse for third place, combined with Simmons's arrangement at the bank, covered the mortgage on Bramwell Field with enough left over to rebuild the hangar roof properly before winter. Her aunt had taken the train in from Wichita without telling her and stood at the fence with Robert Iversen, who had finished second and shook Eleanor's hand rather longer than required, already asking whether she would fly the derby again next year. The Halloway Oil man made good on his word within the week, and a photograph of Eleanor beside the lettered plane ran in three regional papers under a headline about the derby's youngest finisher in the money. Back at the field, Walt had the hands restring the windsock and repaint the hangar doors while she was still signing papers in Wichita, and when she drove up the rutted road and saw the field lit gold in the late afternoon, whole and hers and finally safe, Eleanor Bramwell sat in the truck a moment simply to hold the feeling before stepping out into it.
